The following text is from a story about a fossil collector.

Ada split the gray shale along its seam, and there, pressed flat as a letter in a book, lay a fern frond older than any mountain she had climbed. She tilted it toward the lamp. C.why: You picked the weather sense of "fine." Nothing in the line is about weather. The word describes the veins on a fossil.

D.why: The passage does treat the fossil as a treasure, so this fits the mood. But the word describes what the veins look like, and "valuable as thread" doesn't make sense.

items.stimulus: At dusk the swallows gathered on the telephone wire, and by dark the whole company had settled into silence.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Thomas Arden's 1871 manual on earthworks.

A well-made embankment seldom gives way without first betraying its weakness. Long before the bank fails, an attentive keeper will find a thin seep of water at the toe, a hairline crack along the crest, or a slight bulge where the slope should run straight. These signs are the embankment's own warning, and the engineer who learns to read them may save the work.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "betraying" most nearly mean?
